newsitem.title: UK: UK trade gap widens as buyers lap up imports.
newsitem.headline: UK trade gap widens as buyers lap up imports.

text.p: Britain's trading account with the rest of the world deteriorated in July as a consumer-led economic recovery at home sucked in more goods than were sold abroad, official figures showed on Thursday.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the global trade deficit widened to 1.23 billion pounds ($1.92 billion) from 1.13 billion in June. The deficit was distinctly larger than forecast. City analysts expected the trade gap to narrow to 775 million pounds.
The government shrugged off the data saying it was evidence of the competitive strength of the UK economy.

"This is another set of figures confirming the competitive strength of the UK economy...UK exporters are in an ideal position to benefit from the upturn in our key European markets," said Treasury minister Angela Knight.
The 1.0 percent jump in imports in July compared with June was largely due to consumption of consumer goods from overseas. Demand for clothing from the Far East was a key factor, the ONS said.
Analysts said the figures were disappointing and, with consumer spending likely to accelerate, demand for imports is set to spiral upward later this year.
"The import side is a source of some concern. It's another sign demand for consumer goods is accelerating," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
"While we expect that at this stage of the cycle, if domestic demand holds up it could put pressure on inflation from the costs of imported goods."
Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International, agreed imports are likely to edge up during the rest of the year.
"Our suspicion is that UK activity is picking up quite sharply at the moment and we would expect to see some strong pick-up in imports from our European partners over the next few months."
The trade gap could also come under pressure from higher demand for capital and intermediate goods as the recovery in manufacturing gathers speed.
On the export side, sluggish demand for British goods in the European Union was largely responsible for a tiny 0.3 percent rise in overall sales of British goods abroad in July.
Sharper demand for imports in Europe had been expected to follow the tentative signs of an economic upturn in those economies.
On the ONS's preferred three-month measure, worldwide exports grew 2.5 percent, a fall from 3.0 percent growth recorded in the three months to June.

The figures were early evidence of Britain's trading performance for the third quarter of the year and came only days after current account data for the second quarter showed a dramatic improvement in the trade gap.
The current account went 457 million pounds into the black in three months to June, having spent the previous four quarters in the red.

But incomplete trade data for August also out on Thursday were more encouraging and could signal a bounce back in exports last month. Figures covering trade with countries outside the European Union showed the deficit shrank to 499 million pounds from 688 million in July.
"The trade performance versus the non-EU countries was particularly promising with exports surprisingly robust," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica. ($1=.6416 Pound)
